unit.title: Provide advice to executive team and stakeholders

summary: This unit teaches you to give advice to an executive team (a permanent secretary, a chief executive officer, a board or a minister) and to the stakeholders who are affected by decisions. You will learn to understand what is being asked, gather and analyse evidence, give frank and fearless advice, choose the right form of advice, work with stakeholders, protect confidential information, give timely advice under pressure, manage expectations, and review how good your advice has been.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. Senior officers in ministries, agencies, hospitals, schools and municipal corporations are asked all the time: 'What do you advise?' This unit teaches you to answer well: honestly, clearly, on time and with the evidence to back it up.

The **executive team** is the group that decides: a permanent secretary and directors, a chief executive officer and her managers, or a board. **Stakeholders** are the people and groups who affect, or are affected by, a decision: citizens, staff, unions, contractors, community groups, other agencies and the media. Good advice serves the decision-makers and keeps stakeholders properly informed and consulted.
**Advice** is a professional judgement given to help someone else decide. The adviser analyses, explains and recommends. The executive decides. That line must never be blurred.
**Who it is for:** directors, managers and senior officers who brief executives and deal with stakeholders, and trainees preparing for that role.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Understand the request
Clarify the decision needed, the deadline, the format, the audience and the policy setting before you start.
Gather and analyse evidence
Use sound data and research, compare options against clear criteria, state assumptions and show risk.
Give frank and fearless advice
Give honest, complete advice even when it is unwelcome, respectfully and with evidence, and stay politically neutral.
Choose and prepare the form of advice
Write a brief, a paper or an options paper, or prepare an oral briefing, suited to the audience and time available.
Work with stakeholders
Identify and consult them, build relationships, report back accurately and manage their expectations.
Protect confidentiality and act ethically
Keep information confidential, declare conflicts of interest, refuse gifts and follow the code of conduct.
Give timely advice
Meet deadlines, give interim advice when needed and tell leaders urgent facts straight away.
Keep records and review the advice
File what was advised and why, handle decisions professionally, and learn from feedback and results.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of scenario questions, including simple sums such as cost per person, payback and weighted scores.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as options paper, sensitivity analysis, weighted scoring) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Group practical tasks**: write an advice paper for an executive team, and brief an executive and report back to stakeholders in role plays. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: Advice is only as good as its figures. Work every sum twice, by two different routes, before it goes to the executive.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Understanding the request and your role

blocks.p: Many poor papers answer the wrong question. Before you analyse anything, make sure you understand the request.

head: Ask
Why it matters
Example
rows: What decision is needed?
Advice should help a specific decision, not just describe a topic
'Should we extend clinic hours, and from when?'
By when?
Late advice is useless
'The board meets on Tuesday; papers are due Friday'
In what form?
A one-page brief, a full paper or a verbal briefing
A minister may want one page; a board a full paper
For whom?
Language and detail suit the reader
Board, community leaders, front-line staff
What is the policy setting?
Advice must fit the government's stated priorities, the law and the body's mandate
Government's stated priorities for rural development
What is already decided or known?
Avoids wasting time and shows your starting point
Budget ceiling, earlier studies

blocks.p: A public servant who advises a minister must understand the **government's stated policy priorities**, so that advice is relevant to the decisions being made. Respond to the preferences of the person you advise: if a new chief executive likes short emailed updates and her predecessor liked long reports, adapt to her preference, and keep detail available on request.

head: Role
What it does
rows: Adviser
Analyses, advises and recommends; does not make the decision
Executive team or office holder with authority
Makes the final decision and is accountable for it
Stakeholders
Provide views, are affected, may help or resist implementation
Authorised media officer
Speaks for the body to the media

blocks.p: Public servants serve the Government of the day and must remain **politically neutral**. You advise on the facts and options; you do not campaign for a party or comment on party politics. If a stakeholder group asks which party's housing policy is better, explain the agency's role and stay neutral; you can explain what the agency does and what it does not do.

blocks.note: In the Jamaican public sector, advice to a minister goes through the proper channel, normally the permanent secretary. Follow your ministry's protocol on who may advise whom, and on contact with the media.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Evidence-based advice** rests on sound data, research and analysis. Choose sources that fit the question.

head: Question
Better evidence
Weaker evidence
rows: How many young people are out of work?
National labour force statistics and programme evaluations
A few comments on social media
How do parents feel about a school bus scheme?
A fair sample survey plus route data
The views of the three parents who complained
Does an earlier programme work?
Independent evaluations with a comparison group
The programme manager's own summary

blocks.p: If two studies disagree, do not choose the one you like. **Report both, explain the difference and weigh them.** Always **state your assumptions**, for example 'take-up of 60%', so that the reader can judge how reliable a forecast is.

Present **more than one option** so that decision-makers can weigh real choices and trade-offs. Include keeping the present arrangement. Compare options with the **same criteria**, such as **cost, benefit, risk, fairness and ease of delivery**.

head: Tool
How it works
Worked example
rows: Cost per unit
Total cost divided by the number served
Option costs J$36 m and serves 4,500 households: 36,000,000 / 4,500 = J$8,000 per household
Comparing costs per unit
Compare options with different costs and reach
A: J$45 m for 9,000 farmers = J$5,000 each. B: J$30 m for 5,000 = J$6,000 each. A costs less per farmer
Simple payback
Cost divided by yearly saving
J$15 m cost, saves J$3 m a year: 5 years
Cumulative payback
Add savings year by year when they start late
Cost J$12 m in year 1; saves J$4 m a year from year 2: 4, 8, 12 so by the end of year 4
Benefit-cost ratio
Benefits divided by cost
Cost J$20 m, benefits J$50 m: 2.5
Weighted scoring
Weight each criterion, score each option, multiply and add
Cost 60%, impact 40%; scores 5 and 9: 0.6 x 5 + 0.4 x 9 = 6.6
Percentages
Part divided by whole, times 100
520 of 800 stakeholders support: 65%. 40% of 12,500 households: 5,000
Sensitivity analysis
Show results if a key assumption changes
If take-up could be 40% or 70%, show both and what changes

blocks.p: For **weighted scoring**, agree the criteria and weights before scoring any option, so that the weights are not tuned to a favourite. Show the weights and scores in a table, and point out where a different weight would change the ranking.

Advice should state the **main risks of each option and how to manage them**. For each, say what could go wrong, how likely and how serious it is, and what would reduce it. Where you are unsure about a key figure, show results under both likely cases.

blocks.note: A forecast without its assumptions cannot be checked. A figure without its source cannot be trusted. Put both on the page.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Frank and fearless advice, ethics and integrity

blocks.p: **Frank and fearless advice** means giving honest, complete advice based on the evidence, even when it is unwelcome, without being swayed by what the decision-maker would like to hear. It does **not** mean being rude or hostile: it is given respectfully, privately where appropriate, and with evidence and alternatives.

head: Feature of good advice
Feature of bad advice
rows: Honest about problems and weaknesses
Hides facts that do not fit
Based on evidence
Based on guesses or wishes
Balanced; shows the case for and against
One-sided, selling a favourite option
Gives a clear recommendation
Vague, leaving the reader to guess
Respectful in tone
Insulting, or flattering
Given early, before it is too late to act
Given only when asked, or only when the problem is too big to hide

flow: Check your facts and sources before you speak
Choose the right time and place; go to the person first, not the media
State the main point plainly and show the evidence
Offer options and what you recommend
Acknowledge what is working and why the decision-maker may see it differently
Record your advice and keep to your professional role

blocks.p: **Proactive advice** is given before you are asked, for example to warn of an emerging risk. If monitoring shows a flagship programme will run J$20 million over budget, tell the executive team early, with the causes and options to respond, rather than waiting for the year-end.

head: Situation
What to do
rows: You are asked to advise on a proposal from a firm in which a close relative has an interest
Declare the conflict of interest and step aside from the advice
A firm whose proposal you are assessing offers you an all-expenses-paid trip
Refuse it and report the offer under the code of conduct
A senior colleague asks you to leave out evidence that does not fit the preferred option
Include it and raise your concern through the proper channel
A contractor asks what the agency will recommend on a tender
Decline politely and explain that advice is confidential
You made an error in a figure that has gone to the executive
Tell the executive quickly and send a correction

blocks.note: The test for gifts and hospitality: could it look as though your advice was influenced? If yes, decline and report it. Public bodies have a code of conduct and rules on gifts; follow them.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The executive may reject your recommendation. That is its right. **Accept the decision and help to carry it out well.** Do not undermine it, and do not say 'I told you so'. If you still believe a serious risk is being ignored, put your concern in writing to the right person once and keep a record. Note the decision, the reasons and your advice on file.

sections.title: Forms of advice: writing and briefing

blocks.p: Choose the form that suits the **reader, the time and the decision**.

head: Form
Best when
Key features
rows: One-page brief
A minister or executive has only minutes to read, such as before a press conference
Key facts, the recommendation, and points to say (lines to take)
Briefing paper or advice paper
A full decision needs analysis and a record
Executive summary, analysis, options, risks, recommendation, annexes
Options paper
Several courses of action are possible
Each option with pros, cons, costs and risks; a recommendation
Oral briefing
A short meeting, or an urgent matter
Key points, likely questions and answers prepared; a short written note afterwards
Slide presentation
A group needs to see data, trends or a timeline
Few words, one idea per slide; handouts for detail
Regular update
Progress on an ongoing programme
Progress against plan, issues, decisions needed

ul: **Lead with the main point.** An executive summary should contain the issue, the recommendation and the main reasons.
**Explain technical terms.** A technical brief on water supply for a board should lead with the main point and explain terms.
**Keep sums and sources visible.** Put detail in annexes.
**Adapt to each audience.** The same issue may need a different version for the board, for community leaders and for front-line staff.
**Use plain English** and short sentences.

flow: Open with the main point and the decision needed
Give the two or three key facts
Set out options with the risks and the cost of each
Invite questions and answer honestly, including what is not yet known
Confirm the decision and the next steps; follow up in writing

blocks.p: Prepare for a ten-minute briefing with **key points, likely questions and answers**, not a long script. Check the room and any slides. If you do not know an answer, say so and promise a date for the answer; do not guess.

Where the executive asks for weekly updates on a recovery programme, the useful update shows **progress against plan, issues and decisions needed**. Keep the format the same each week so changes stand out.

blocks.note: A good one-page brief to a minister has the headline, the background in two or three lines, the recommendation, the main risk, and two or three lines to take. If it needs more than a page, it needs more thinking.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Advice often depends on people outside the executive team. Involve them early and properly.
**Stakeholder analysis** lists every group affected or able to influence a decision, and rates each one's **interest** and **power or influence**. It tells you who needs what kind of contact.

head: Group
Power / influence
Interest
How to deal with them
rows: High power, high interest
High
High
Manage closely: involve in the work, consult early and often
High power, low interest
High
Low
Keep satisfied: brief on key points, no overload
Low power, high interest
Low
High
Keep informed and listen: they often notice problems
Low power, low interest
Low
Low
Monitor: general information

blocks.p: Consulting before deciding helps you **understand the effects and raise issues before the decision is made**. It makes the decision better, and it builds **buy-in**, which is the support and acceptance of the people affected. An executive that decides without consulting parents, schools and bus operators may find the scheme fails in practice.

head: Method
Good for
Take care that
rows: Meetings and forums
Open discussion with many people
Quiet voices are heard, not only the loudest
Written submissions
Detailed views and a record
Give clear questions and a deadline
Surveys
Numbers from a wide group
The sample is fair
One-to-one meetings
Sensitive issues, key leaders
Notes are taken
Focus groups
Reasons behind views
Groups are chosen to be mixed or separate as needed

blocks.p: Build **trust before you need it**. A director who knows the leaders of the farmers' associations, the churches and the unions can consult quickly and hear frank views when something urgent comes up.

blocks.h: Representing the agency at a forum

blocks.p: If the executive asks you to represent the agency at a stakeholder forum, make clear in advance what you may say and not say. Afterwards report back to the executive: **the main views, any agreements and the issues to decide.** Do not commit the agency to anything you are not authorised to promise.
If advice on a road project will also affect the water agency and the housing agency, **consult the other agencies and reflect their views** in your advice.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, the Social Development Commission and municipal corporations know many community groups; trade unions and professional bodies are consulted on changes that affect their members, as agreements require.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Advice has a deadline. If the executive meets on Monday to decide a budget item and your full analysis will not be ready until Wednesday, **give interim advice and state its limits clearly**. Do not hold back, and do not pretend that incomplete analysis is complete.

head: Situation
What to do
rows: A serious matter arises out of hours, such as a data breach at 6 p.m.
Tell the chief executive officer straight away, with the facts known so far; add more as you learn it
A decision must be made within hours with incomplete information
Give the best advice from what is known, say what is unknown and what assumptions you made, recommend a safe first step and how to review it
Papers are due 7 days before a meeting
Work back from the meeting date and set your own earlier deadlines for checks
You find an error after sending advice
Tell the executive quickly and send a correction

blocks.p: **Confidential** information must not be shared beyond the people entitled to see it. Advice to the executive, draft papers, tender information and personal data are usually confidential until released by the proper authority.

ul: **Need to know**: share only with people who need it for their work.
**Contractors and stakeholders** who ask what you will recommend: decline and explain that advice is confidential. Offer another way for them to give their views.
**Journalists**: refer calls to the authorised media officer.
**Personal information**: use only what is needed and remove names where possible. Check the body's duties under the data protection law, which exists to protect personal data and limit its use.
**Storage**: use secure systems, mark papers 'confidential' and do not leave them on printers or in public places.
**Sharing with partners**: check it is lawful before sharing client records with a private partner.

blocks.p: Keep **records of advice**: what was advised, when, to whom and on what evidence. They show how a decision was reached, protect you and the body when questions are asked later, and help future advisers. Use **records management**: a system for filing and keeping records so they can be found later, with version control for drafts and a clear rule for how long they are kept.

blocks.note: A decision that cannot be traced to advice and evidence is hard to defend to an auditor, a minister or the public. Record the date, the options considered, the advice and the decision.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Managing expectations, decisions and reviewing your advice

blocks.p: Stakeholders may expect more than the body can deliver. Honest, early and clear communication protects trust.

head: Situation
Good response
rows: A community group expects the agency to fund its whole proposal, but only part is approved
Explain the decision honestly, what is possible and what the next steps are
A stakeholder asks you to promise that the executive will approve a project
Explain that you advise but the executive decides; say when the decision is expected
Two groups want the same limited resource, such as water for farms and for hotels
Set out both interests, the trade-offs and the options for the executive; do not take sides secretly
The decision goes against a stakeholder's wishes
Explain the decision and reasons clearly, without blaming the executive and without promising what you cannot deliver

blocks.p: Never promise a result you do not control. Be clear about timescales, what is decided and what is still open.
Good advisers check whether their advice is useful. Methods:

ul: **Ask the executive team for feedback**: was it clear, timely, balanced and useful?
**Note how advice was used**: was it accepted, changed or rejected, and why?
**Review results** some months after a decision: are the expected results being achieved? (For example, six months after an executive accepted a recommendation.)
**Review a sample of papers** for accuracy, clarity and timeliness against an agreed checklist.
**Track measures**: the percentage delivered on time, the percentage rated useful (18 of 24 papers rated useful is 75%), and the number of errors corrected.
**Share lessons** in the unit and update templates.

flow: Write or brief with a clear recommendation
Record and follow up the decision

blocks.note: Professionals are judged by how they behave when advice is not taken, not only when it is. Stay courteous, help to deliver the decision and keep the record straight.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: clarify a request: the decision needed, the deadline, the format and the audience.
explain the roles of adviser, executive and stakeholders, and why public servants stay politically neutral.
choose suitable evidence, report conflicting studies fairly and state assumptions.
compare options on cost, benefit, risk, fairness and ease of delivery.
work cost per unit, payback, benefit-cost ratio, weighted scores and percentages, checking twice.
show risk and use sensitivity analysis where a key figure is uncertain.
give frank and fearless advice respectfully, and give proactive advice early.
handle conflicts of interest, gifts and pressure to leave out evidence correctly.
choose between a one-page brief, an advice paper, an options paper, an oral briefing and slides.
prepare an oral briefing with key points and likely questions.
carry out stakeholder analysis and consult in ways that build buy-in.
give interim and urgent advice with its limits stated.
protect confidential and personal information and keep proper records.
manage stakeholder expectations without promising what I cannot deliver.
accept decisions professionally and review the quality of my advice.

terms: Executive team
The group or office holder with authority to make the decision.
Stakeholder
A person or group that affects, or is affected by, a decision.
Frank and fearless advice
Honest, complete advice given even when unwelcome.
Proactive advice
Advice offered before it is asked for, for example to warn of a risk.
Political neutrality
Serving the Government of the day impartially, without party politics.
Options paper
A paper that sets out several courses of action with pros and cons.
Lines to take
Short suggested statements for a minister or officer to use with the media.
Stakeholder analysis
Listing affected groups and rating their interest and influence.
Buy-in
The support and acceptance of people affected by a decision.
Weighted scoring
Comparing options by scoring them against weighted criteria.
Sensitivity analysis
Showing how results change when a key assumption changes.
Payback period
Cost divided by the yearly saving.
Confidential
Not to be shared beyond those entitled to see it.
Records management
The system for filing and keeping records so they can be found later.
Interim advice
Advice given before the full analysis is finished, with its limits stated.

c1.title: Extending clinic hours in St Thomas
c1.text: The executive team of a regional health authority must decide how to improve evening access to primary care in St Thomas. Option A: extend hours at four health centres, J$9 million a year, expecting 6,000 extra patient visits. Option B: a mobile clinic, J$14 million a year, expecting 7,000 extra visits. Option C: keep present arrangements, no extra cost and almost no extra visits. The adviser, Natalie Gordon, scores the options out of 10 using weights of cost 50%, access 30% and ease of delivery 20%. Option A scores 8, 6 and 9; Option B scores 5, 9 and 5; Option C scores 10, 1 and 10. She is not sure whether A will really draw 6,000 visits; it may be as low as 4,500.

c2.title: A proposed waste transfer station near a community
c2.text: A municipal corporation in St Catherine plans to build a waste transfer station near a settlement of about 900 households. The corporation's executive has asked the director, Mr Richard Palmer, to advise on the plan. Groups affected include the residents, a farmers' cooperative next door, the parish health department, the contractor hoping to build it, a church and the national environment agency, which must be consulted on environmental approval. A resident at a meeting demands, 'Promise us now that it will not be built here.'

c3.title: A youth skills programme running behind
c3.text: A ministry's youth skills programme has a budget of J$50 million for 12 months and a target of enrolling 1,000 trainees. After six months J$38 million has been spent and 420 trainees are enrolled. The head of the programme tells the director, Ms Joan Francis, 'Keep this out of the quarterly board pack; we will fix it before the next one.' Ms Francis's analysis shows that if spending continues at the same rate, the budget will be exceeded.

c4.title: A suspected contamination of a community water supply
c4.text: At 4 p.m. a parish health officer reports that 2 of 5 water samples from a community supply tested positive for a harmful bacterium. Results for 3 samples will not be available until tomorrow morning. The permanent secretary's executive team will meet at 6 p.m. and must decide whether to issue a boil-water notice to 2,000 residents. The director of environmental health, Mr Everton Smith, is asked to advise.

c5.title: Advice unit in a social services ministry
c5.text: A policy and advice unit in a ministry holds draft papers for the executive and a database of 12,000 beneficiaries of a social assistance programme. A non-governmental organisation asks a junior officer for a copy of a draft paper on proposed changes to the programme. A consultant asks for the full beneficiary file, with names, to check a sample. The unit head wants to measure how good the unit's advice is: last quarter the unit sent 24 papers; 18 were rated useful by the executive in a feedback form.

questions.q: What is the cost per extra patient visit for Option A?
questions.why: J$9,000,000 divided by 6,000 visits is J$1,500 per visit. Option B is J$14,000,000 / 7,000 = J$2,000.

questions.q: What is Option B's weighted score?
Which statement should Natalie put in her paper about the scoring?
o: Option A ranks first on these weights, and the weights were agreed before scoring
Option C ranks first because it costs nothing and so cost is the only fair criterion
Option B ranks first because it brings the most extra visits of all three options
Weights are not needed, because the scores alone show the best option
questions.why: A scores 7.6, C 7.3 and B 6.2. Weights should be agreed before scoring and shown, so readers can see how the ranking was reached and test other weights.

questions.q: Natalie is unsure whether A will draw 6,000 or only 4,500 visits. What should her advice do?
o: Show results at both levels, such as J$2,000 per visit at 4,500, and say what changes
Use 6,000 only, since the authority's own planning figure is the one it should rely on
Use 4,500 only, since a cautious figure is always the safer one to put before a board
Leave out the cost per visit altogether because the number is uncertain
questions.why: 9,000,000 / 4,500 = J$2,000, equal to B's cost at its estimate. Sensitivity analysis shows how results change with the assumption so decision-makers can see the risk.

questions.q: Where would Mr Palmer place the residents on a power-interest grid, and how should they be dealt with?
o: High interest and real influence through organising, so consult them closely and early
Low interest, as they are outside the corporation, so inform them after the decision
Low interest, as there are too many of them to consult in any meaningful way
High formal power over the decision, so they should be asked to choose the site
questions.why: Residents are directly affected (high interest) and can organise and object, so they have real influence. Consult them early; they do not make the formal decision, which belongs to the executive.

questions.q: Why should the corporation consult residents, the cooperative and the health department before advising the executive?
o: To understand the effects and raise issues before the decision is made
To avoid the need for any environmental approval process on the site
To show the contractor which residents are most likely to object
To make the executive's decision final before any meeting is held
questions.why: Consultation before deciding improves advice and builds buy-in. It does not replace statutory approval, reveal confidential material or pre-empt the executive.

questions.q: How should the officer at the meeting respond to the resident's demand for a promise?
o: Explain that the executive decides, describe the process and say when views will be heard
Promise that the station will be built elsewhere, to calm the meeting down
Promise that it will be built here, so that residents know where they stand
Say nothing and let the meeting end without giving any reply at all
questions.why: An adviser or officer cannot promise what the decision-maker has not decided. Explain the process and timeline honestly, and record the concern for the executive.

questions.q: The farmers' cooperative next door has a lot of influence but says it is too busy to attend public meetings. What is the best approach?
o: Meet its leaders one-to-one and keep them informed in writing
Leave it out, since it did not come to the meetings it was invited to
Wait until the decision is made and then send a letter
Ask the residents to speak for the cooperative at the forum
questions.why: A high-influence group must not be ignored because it avoids public meetings. Adapt the method (a private meeting, written updates) so its views reach the advice.

questions.q: What percentage of the target enrolment has been reached after six months?
questions.why: 420 / 1,000 = 0.42 or 42%. (76% is the share of the budget spent, 38 / 50.)

questions.q: If spending continues at the same rate, by how much will the programme exceed its J$50 million budget?
o: J$26 million
J$38 million
J$12 million
J$76 million
questions.why: J$38 million in six months is J$76 million in twelve. 76 - 50 = J$26 million over. J$76 million is the total, not the overspend.

questions.q: The programme head asks Ms Francis to leave the problem out of the board pack. What should she do?
o: Report it with causes and options, and raise her concern with the head and the executive
Leave it out, and mention it in the next pack as the programme head suggests
Report it to the newspapers so that the public knows the real position
Report the enrolment figure only and leave out the spending figures
questions.why: Frank and fearless advice tells the executive early, with causes and options to respond. Hiding facts or going to the media are both wrong; use the proper channels.

questions.q: The board hears the advice and decides to continue the programme unchanged, against Ms Francis's recommendation. What should she do?
o: Accept the decision, record her advice and help to carry it out
Refuse to work on the programme any longer as a matter of principle
Tell her staff that the board has made a mistake in its decision
Quietly slow down the work to show that the board was wrong
questions.why: The executive decides. A professional accepts the decision, keeps a record of the advice and helps it to succeed, while continuing to report honestly on the results.

questions.q: Only two results are in. How should Mr Smith advise the 6 p.m. meeting?
o: Give interim advice, say what is known and not known, and recommend a precaution
Say that no advice is possible until all five results arrive tomorrow morning
Advise that the water is safe, since the other three samples might be clear
Advise that results be kept from residents until they have all been confirmed
questions.why: When a decision cannot wait, give the best advice on the evidence, state the limits and recommend a safe first step. Delay may harm residents; false reassurance is dishonest.

questions.q: Which form of advice best suits this meeting?
o: A short oral briefing with a one-page note of facts, options and recommendation
A 30-page report with full annexes, to be sent to the executive tomorrow
A slide presentation of 40 slides setting out the laboratory methods used
A telephone message left with the permanent secretary's driver
questions.why: With two hours to go, an oral briefing backed by a one-page note leads with the main point and gives the decision-makers what they need. Long papers come later.

questions.q: Which statement should Mr Smith make clear about the evidence?
o: 2 of 5 samples are positive, 3 are pending, and the advice may change
All of the water in the system is contaminated, as some of it clearly is
The results do not matter until every one of them has been received
The pending results will almost certainly be negative
questions.why: Honest advice states what is known, what is not and what could change. It does not overstate or understate the evidence.

questions.q: What should be recorded after the meeting?
o: The advice, the evidence and assumptions, the decision and who took it
The decision only, because the advice is not needed once it is taken
The names of the people who attended the meeting and the time it ended
Nothing, because the decision had to be made in such a hurry
questions.why: Records show what was advised, when, and on what evidence. They matter most for urgent decisions made with incomplete information.

questions.q: What should the junior officer do about the NGO's request for the draft paper?
o: Decline politely, explain that drafts are confidential and offer another way to comment
Send the draft, because the NGO speaks for people who may be affected by the changes
Send the draft with the sensitive sections removed, without asking anyone first
Ignore the request and say nothing about it to anyone
questions.why: Draft advice to the executive is confidential until released through the proper channel. Offer the NGO a way to give its views, and refer the matter to the unit head.

questions.q: How should the unit respond to the consultant's request for the full beneficiary file with names?
o: Supply only the data needed, names removed where possible, with authority and safeguards
Supply the whole file at once, as consultants working for the ministry are trusted
Refuse to share data with anybody inside or outside the ministry for any reason
Email the complete file to the consultant's own personal address
questions.why: The data protection law's purpose is to protect personal data and limit its use. Share only what is needed, remove names where possible and use secure channels.

questions.q: What percentage of the unit's papers were rated useful, and what should the unit also do?
o: 75%, and also look at why the others were not rated useful
75%, which is a perfect result so there is nothing more to learn
18%, because 18 papers were rated useful
25%, because that is the share of papers that were not
questions.why: 18 / 24 = 0.75, or 75%. A good result still leaves 6 papers; the unit should ask why they were not rated useful and use the feedback to improve.

questions.q: Which practice best helps the unit show later what it advised, and on what evidence?
o: Records management: papers filed with dates, versions and the evidence used
Keeping each draft on the personal computer of the officer who wrote it
Relying on officers to remember what was advised and why
Deleting drafts once the final version has been sent to the executive
questions.why: Records management lets advice, evidence and decisions be found later. Scattered files and memory cannot show how a decision was reached.
